title: Why does music move us? With Robert Zatorre, PhD

sentences.en: Do you get chills when you hear the chorale from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony?
sentences.zh: 当你听到贝多芬第九交响曲的合唱时，会感到寒毛直竖吗？

sentences.en: Does Samuel Barber's adagio for strings make you tear up?
sentences.zh: 塞缪尔·巴伯的《弦乐柔板》会让你感动得落泪吗？

sentences.en: Are there songs that transport you to another time, whether it's music by the Beatles or the police or Nirvana?
sentences.zh: 有没有哪首歌能把你带到另一个时代，无论是披头士、警察乐队还是涅槃乐队的音乐？

sentences.en: Does some music make you happy and want to dance?
sentences.zh: 有些音乐会让你感到快乐并想要跳舞吗？

sentences.en: For many of us, music taps into our deepest emotions and memories.
sentences.zh: 对我们许多人来说，音乐触及了我们最深的情感和记忆。

sentences.en: And yet, for others, music is just meh.
sentences.zh: 然而，对其他人而言，音乐就只是平平无奇。

sentences.en: Over the last several decades, psychologists and other researchers have begun to explore why music affects us so profoundly.
sentences.zh: 在过去的几十年里，心理学家和其他研究人员开始探索为什么音乐对我们有着如此深远的影响。

sentences.en: What happens in the brain when we listen to music or when we sing or play an instrument?
sentences.zh: 当我们听音乐、唱歌或演奏乐器时，大脑中发生了什么？

sentences.en: Why does some music give us goosebumps while other pieces leave us cold?
sentences.zh: 为什么有些音乐会让我们起鸡皮疙瘩，而另一些作品却让我们无动于衷？

sentences.en: On the other hand, why do a small number of people experience almost no emotional response to music at all?
sentences.zh: 另一方面，为什么极少数人对音乐几乎完全没有情感反应？

sentences.en: And what can studying music and the brain teach us about broader questions of perception, memory, language, and cognition?
sentences.zh: 研究音乐与大脑能为我们理解感知、记忆、语言和认知等更广泛的问题提供什么启示？

sentences.en: Welcome to Speaking of Psychology, the flagship podcast of the American Psychological Association that examines the links between psychological science and everyday life.
sentences.zh: 欢迎收听《心理学说话》，这是美国心理学协会的旗舰播客，旨在探讨心理科学与日常生活之间的联系。

sentences.en: I'm Kim Mills.
sentences.zh: 我是金·米尔斯。

sentences.en: My guest today is Dr. Robert Zatori, a professor in the Department of Neurology and Neurosurgery at McGill University,
sentences.zh: 我今天的嘉宾是罗伯特·扎托雷博士，他是麦吉尔大学神经学和神经外科系的教授，

sentences.en: who holds a Canada Research Chair in Auditory and Cognitive Neuroscience at the Montreal Neurological Institute.
sentences.zh: 并在蒙特利尔神经学研究所担任加拿大听觉与认知神经科学研究讲席教授。

sentences.en: For decades, he's been a pioneer in the neuroscience of music, studying how the brain processes music, speech, and sound,
sentences.zh: 几十年来，他一直是音乐神经科学的先驱，研究大脑如何处理音乐、语言和声音，

sentences.en: and why music can evoke such powerful emotional experiences.
sentences.zh: 以及为什么音乐能够唤起如此强烈的情感体验。

sentences.en: His research has helped to explain how the brain's auditory and reward systems work together to create musical pleasure.
sentences.zh: 他的研究有助于解释大脑的听觉和奖赏系统如何协同工作以产生音乐的愉悦感。

sentences.en: He's examined topics ranging from musical anhedonia, the inability to derive pleasure from music, to the relationship between music and language.
sentences.zh: 他研究过从音乐性快感缺失（即无法从音乐中获得快乐）到音乐与语言关系等各种课题。

sentences.en: He's author of more than 350 scientific research papers, as well as the book, From Perception to Pleasure, The Neuroscience of Music and Why We Love It.
sentences.zh: 他是350多篇科学研究论文的作者，著有《从感知到快乐：音乐神经科学与我们为何热爱音乐》一书。

sentences.en: Dr. Zatori, thank you for joining me today.
sentences.zh: 扎托雷博士，非常感谢你今天能来参加我的节目。

sentences.en: Thank you very much for having me, Kim.
sentences.zh: 非常感谢邀请我，金。

sentences.en: Let's start with a big picture question.
sentences.zh: 让我们从一个宏观的问题开始。

sentences.en: I read in a previous interview that you said music touches every cognitive function there is.
sentences.zh: 我在之前的采访中读到你说，音乐触及了现有的每一项认知功能。

sentences.en: Can you talk about that?
sentences.zh: 你能谈谈这个吗？

sentences.en: How does music touch so many different aspects of human cognition?
sentences.zh: 音乐是如何触及人类认知的如此多的不同方面的？

sentences.en: Part of the reason I say that is when people ask me, well, you know, what's the value of studying music scientifically?
sentences.zh: 我这么说的一部分原因在于，当人们问我，科学研究音乐的价值到底在哪里时，

sentences.en: I often like to point out that music is not merely a pattern of sounds.
sentences.zh: 我经常喜欢指出，音乐不仅仅是一种声音模式。

sentences.en: It is that, of course, but that's just a start.
sentences.zh: 当然，它确实是，但这只是个开始。

sentences.en: And so we can use music to understand the auditory system.
sentences.zh: 因此，我们可以利用音乐来理解听觉系统。

sentences.en: Absolutely, that's a key feature.
sentences.zh: 当然，这是一个关键特征。

sentences.en: But at the same time, music engages many, many, many other functions.
sentences.zh: 但与此同时，音乐还参与了许许多多其他的功能。

sentences.en: So if you consider, for example, an everyday situation, you're waiting for an elevator and
sentences.zh: 所以，如果你考虑一个日常情况，比如你在等电梯，

sentences.en: somebody walks by and they're whistling a tune and you recognize the tune, even though you have never heard it being whistled before.
sentences.zh: 有人从旁走过，吹着一首曲子，你认出了这首曲子，尽管你以前从听过别人吹这首曲子。

sentences.en: You know what it is.
sentences.zh: 你知道那是什么。

sentences.en: Sometimes you immediately think of the fact that it was being played last summer when you were at the beach with your best friend that you hadn't seen for a while.
sentences.zh: 有时你会立刻联想起，去年夏天你和那位好久不见的挚友在海滩上时，这首歌正在播放。

sentences.en: This brings back memories.
sentences.zh: 这勾起了回忆。

sentences.en: At the same time, you start to tap your foot as you imagine the music.
sentences.zh: 与此同时，当你想象音乐时，你开始用脚打拍子。

sentences.en: So even though the music is gone, the person walked by, you can still actually hear it in your mind's ear.
sentences.zh: 所以，即使音乐已经消失了，那个人已经走过去了，你其实仍然可以在脑海中听到它。

sentences.en: As you do so, you might tap your foot.
sentences.zh: 当你这样做的时候，你可能会用脚打拍子。

sentences.en: You might sway to the rhythm of the music, engaging your motor system, and it may also just be a very pleasurable experience.
sentences.zh: 你可能会随着音乐的节奏摇摆，这调动了你的运动系统，而且它也可能是一种非常愉悦的体验。

sentences.en: You may actually find that you're in a better mood just because you were thinking of that music.
sentences.zh: 你甚至会发现自己心情变好了，仅仅因为你在想那段音乐。

sentences.en: So just think of all the list of cognitive operations that went through there.
sentences.zh: 所以，想想刚才经历过的所有认知操作列表。

sentences.en: There's some kind of auditory processing.
sentences.zh: 某种听觉处理。

sentences.en: There's some engagement with the motor system.
sentences.zh: 某种与运动系统的互动。

sentences.en: There's an engagement with the memory system.
sentences.zh: 某种与记忆系统的互动。

sentences.en: There's an affective response, a hedonic response, an emotional response, etc.
sentences.zh: 某种情感反应、快乐反应、情绪反应等等。

sentences.en: So this is why I like to say it engages the whole brain in the sense that it is a very complex type of human activity
sentences.zh: 这就是为什么我喜欢说它调动了整个大脑，因为它是一种非常复杂的人类活动，

sentences.en: that doesn't stop just at the level of sound, but it is really, I think, remarkably interesting from that perspective because it is so rich.
sentences.zh: 它不仅停留在声音的层面上，而且从这个角度来看，我认为它非常引人入胜，因为它太丰富了。

sentences.en: Now, you found in your research that there's a link between music and pleasure that can be traced to the brain's reward system.
sentences.zh: 你在研究中发现，音乐和快乐之间存在一种联系，可以追溯到大脑的奖赏系统。

sentences.en: How does that work?
sentences.zh: 这是如何运作的？

sentences.en: What's happening in the brain when we're enjoying listening to music?
sentences.zh: 当我们享受听音乐时，大脑中发生了什么？

sentences.en: Yeah, so this is a very, very important part of our research.
sentences.zh: 对，这是我们研究中非常非常重要的一部分。

sentences.en: For years, psychologists and physiologists had studied the so-called reward system.
sentences.zh: 多年来，心理学家和生理学家一直在研究所谓的奖赏系统。

sentences.en: This is a series of structures in the brain that are known to be very important for reward.
sentences.zh: 这是大脑中一系列已知对奖赏非常重要的结构。

sentences.en: So what does reward mean?
sentences.zh: 那么奖赏意味着什么？

sentences.en: In the classical psychology sense, it means a reinforcer.
sentences.zh: 在古典心理学的意义上，它意味着一种强化物。

sentences.en: It means a stimulus that causes the behavior to be repeated.
sentences.zh: 它意味着一种促使行为重复的刺激。

sentences.en: But there's also a hedonic part to it.
sentences.zh: 但它也有快乐的部分。

sentences.en: So although the behaviorists didn't like to talk about that, cognitive psychologists do like to talk about emotions.
sentences.zh: 因此，尽管行为主义者不喜欢谈论这一点，但认知心理学家确实喜欢谈论情绪。

sentences.en: And when there is a rewarding stimulus, it is typically pleasurable.
sentences.zh: 当出现一种奖赏性刺激时，它通常是令人愉悦的。

sentences.en: You feel a sense of pleasure.
sentences.zh: 你会感到一种快乐感。

sentences.en: It's positive in some way.
sentences.zh: 它在某种程度上是积极的。

sentences.en: And all of these sorts of effects have been traced to dopaminergic neurons in certain structures, in the striatum in particular, which is a deep nucleus in the brain,
sentences.zh: 所有这些效应都可以追溯到某些结构中的多巴胺能神经元，特别是纹状体（大脑深处的一个核团），

sentences.en: as well as other parts of the brain, the orbitofrontal cortex and the amygdala and ventral tegmental area.
sentences.zh: 以及大脑的其他部分，如眶额皮层、杏仁核和腹侧被盖区。

sentences.en: There's a whole complex circuitry.
sentences.zh: 这是一个极其复杂的回路。

sentences.en: Now, about 25 years ago, we discovered that music actually activates the same reward system as had been identified for other types of rewarding stimuli.
sentences.zh: 大约25年前，我们发现音乐实际上激活了与其他类型奖赏刺激相同的奖赏系统。

sentences.en: So essentially, there's a single reward system that responds both to primary rewards, things like food, for example.
sentences.zh: 因此，从本质上讲，有一个单一的奖赏系统，它既对主要奖赏（例如食物等事物）作出反应。

sentences.en: If you take a hungry animal and you measure its response to food by putting an electrode into its brain,
sentences.zh: 如果你把一只饥饿的动物抓来，通过把电极插入它的大脑来测量它对食物的反应，

sentences.en: you will see that those dopamine neurons are very active when the food is delivered.
sentences.zh: 你会发现当食物送达时，那些多巴胺神经元非常活跃。

sentences.en: Nobody really knew, including us, when we discovered it, that a completely abstract stimulus like music could also engage that system.
sentences.zh: 在发现之前，包括我们在内的任何人都没有真正料到，像音乐这样完全抽象的刺激也能激活该系统。

sentences.en: But indeed, that is what we found using brain imaging techniques.
sentences.zh: 但事实确实如此，这是我们使用脑成像技术发现的。

sentences.en: And then a few years later, we were able to demonstrate that the response is actually driven by dopamine neurons.
sentences.zh: 几年后，我们能够证明这种反应实际上是由多巴胺神经元驱动的。

sentences.en: We know this because we can use technology to measure dopamine response in the brain non-invasively.
sentences.zh: 我们之所以知道这一点，是因为我们可以利用技术以无创的方式测量大脑中的多巴胺反应。

sentences.en: We have positron emission tomography, which is a way of measuring the chemical activity in the brain.
sentences.zh: 我们有正电子发射断层扫描（PET），这是一种测量大脑化学活动的方法。

sentences.en: And more recently, with some colleagues in Spain, we did some experiments where we manipulated the dopamine levels pharmacologically
sentences.zh: 最近，我们与西班牙的一些同事做了一些实验，通过药理学方法操纵多巴胺水平，

sentences.en: by giving volunteers certain drugs that would either elevate or inhibit the dopamine system.
sentences.zh: 给志愿者服用某些药物，这些药物要么提高、要么抑制多巴胺系统。

sentences.en: And we found that, indeed, music given after the administration of the dopamine precursor actually gave more pleasure.
sentences.zh: 我们发现，在给予多巴胺前体后听音乐，确实能带来更多的快乐。

sentences.en: And when you gave the dopamine inhibitor, it actually resulted in less pleasure.
sentences.zh: 而当你给予多巴胺抑制剂时，它实际上会导致更少的快乐。

sentences.en: So this links music to all of these more biologically given sorts of stimuli and I think raises very interesting questions about,
sentences.zh: 因此，这把音乐与所有这些更具生物学基础的刺激联系在了一起，我认为这也提出了非常有趣的问题：

sentences.en: you know, how is it that our brains are able to respond to this completely abstract stimulus that we call music?
sentences.zh: 我们的а大脑怎么能够对这种我们称之为音乐的完全抽象的刺激作出反应？

sentences.en: And it's not just music, by the way, it's other art forms as well.
sentences.zh: 顺便说一句，不仅是音乐，还有其他艺术形式也是如此。

sentences.en: And how is it that this very kind of primal survival-related mechanism is brought into play?
sentences.zh: 这种与生俱来的生存相关机制是如何被调动起来的？

sentences.en: And I think that's a topic, you know, that we're very actively pursuing, we and many other laboratories around the world.
sentences.zh: 我认为这是一个我们以及世界各地许多实验室正在积极探讨的课题。

sentences.en: So what you described just was about appreciation of music, reaction to hearing music.
sentences.zh: 你刚才描述的只是关于对音乐的欣赏，对听音乐的反应。

sentences.en: But what about producing music?
sentences.zh: 但是创作音乐呢？

sentences.en: Is there a structure in the brain that's responsible for musical comprehension?
sentences.zh: 大脑中是否存在负责音乐理解的结构？

sentences.en: Well, there's actually a very, very tight coupling between the auditory system and the motor system.
sentences.zh: 嗯，实际上听觉系统和运动系统之间存在着非常非常紧密的耦合。

sentences.en: So we can see that if we measure, for example, brain oscillations in the motor part of the brain, the part that controls the muscles and the auditory part of the brain,
sentences.zh: 因此我们可以看到，如果我们测量例如大脑运动部分（控制肌肉的部分）和听觉部分（

sentences.en: the part that is responsible for processing sound, we see that the oscillations are very strongly coupled.
sentences.zh: 负责处理声音的部分）的脑振荡，我们会发现这些振荡耦合得非常强烈。

sentences.en: They're in phase with each other between the auditory and the motor system in a way that doesn't quite happen, for example, if you look at the visual and the motor system.
sentences.zh: 听觉系统和运动系统之间的振荡是同相的，这种现象在视觉和运动系统之间是不会发生的。

sentences.en: So they're not as strongly coupled as they are for the auditory and motor.
sentences.zh: 所以它们的耦合程度不如听觉和运动系统那样强。

sentences.en: And we think that this means that there's a very close relationship between perceiving sounds and generating sounds.
sentences.zh: 我们认为这意味着感知声音和产生声音之间存在着非常紧密的联系。

sentences.en: If you think about it for a moment, basically every sound that you hear is the outcome of some action.
sentences.zh: 如果你仔细想想，基本上你听到的每一个声音都是某种动作的结果。

sentences.en: There can't be sound if no action has occurred, with some very, very slight exceptions, like, I don't know, thunder.
sentences.zh: 如果没有发生任何动作，就不会有声音，除了某些非常非常微小的例外，比如，我不知道，雷声。

sentences.en: And even then, there's some action in the cloud.
sentences.zh: 即便如此，云层中也有一些动作。

sentences.en: There's some kind of interaction between the molecules.
sentences.zh: 分子之间存在某种相互作用。

sentences.en: So if you have a completely static environment where nothing is changing, it'll be a silent environment.
sentences.zh: 因此，如果你有一个完全静态、没有任何变化的环境，那将是一个寂静的环境。

sentences.en: So already, at the level of sort of physics, there's a close link there.
sentences.zh: 所以，从物理学的层面来看，它们之间已经存在着紧密的联系。

sentences.en: And if you think about it from terms of biology, many, many actions, not all, but many actions produce sound.
sentences.zh: 如果你从生物学的角度来思考，许多、许多动作（并非全部，但很多动作）都会产生声音。

sentences.en: Including, you know, when we speak, right?
sentences.zh: 包括，你知道的，我们说话的时候，对吧？

sentences.en: Right now, I'm moving my lips and my tongue and my larynx in a coordinated manner to produce certain types of sounds.
sentences.zh: 现在，我正在以协调的方式移动我的嘴唇、舌头和喉部，以产生特定类型的声音。

sentences.en: Same thing when I walk.
sentences.zh: 我走路时也是如此。

sentences.en: When I walk, you hear footsteps.
sentences.zh: 当我走路时，你能听到脚步声。

sentences.en: If I clap, you hear sounds, right?
sentences.zh: 如果我鼓掌，你能听到声音，对吧？

sentences.en: So all those sounds are the outcome of different kinds of actions.
sentences.zh: 所以所有这些声音都是不同动作的结果。

sentences.en: And I think if we think about it from sort of a biological perspective, this is something that's very, very fundamental.
sentences.zh: 我认为如果我们从某种生物学的角度来思考，这是非常非常根本的东西。

sentences.en: From the first moments of life, we hear sounds that we produce ourselves, right?
sentences.zh: 从生命的最初时刻起，我们就听到了自己产生的声音，对吧？

sentences.en: What's the first thing that an infant does upon emerging from the womb?
sentences.zh: 婴儿从子宫里出来后做的第一件事是什么？

sentences.en: It screaMs.
sentences.zh: 它尖叫。

sentences.en: If it's healthy, that's what it will do, right?
sentences.zh: 如果它很健康，它就会这么做，对吧？

sentences.en: So literally, from the first moment, you're activating your vocal tract and producing sound.
sentences.zh: 所以字面意义上，从最初的那一刻起，你就在激活你的声道并发出声音。

sentences.en: And so this, I think, is kind of a very, very basic level is the link between movement, action, and sound.
sentences.zh: 因此，我认为这是一个非常非常基础的层面，即运动、动作和声音之间的联系。

sentences.en: And also, these things influence each other.
sentences.zh: 而且，这些事物会相互影响。

sentences.en: So if I'm playing a musical instrument or if I'm speaking, the action that I make will produce a certain sound.
sentences.zh: 所以，如果我在演奏乐器或者在说话，我所做的动作会产生某种声音。

sentences.en: But if I'm playing an instrument, for example, I have a certain target in mind.
sentences.zh: 但如果我在演奏乐器，比如说，我心里有一个特定的目标。

sentences.en: The sound is supposed to be a certain note with a certain tone.
sentences.zh: 声音应该是一个带有特定音色的特定音符。

sentences.en: So as I'm playing, let's say I'm playing a violin, as I'm drawing the bow across the strings, I'm listening to the sound.
sentences.zh: 所以当我演奏时，比方说我在拉小提琴，当我把琴弓拉过琴弦时，我在听着声音。

sentences.en: If it's not what I wanted, my auditory system will feed back to the motor system and say,
sentences.zh: 如果它不是我想要的，我的听觉系统会向运动系统反馈并说：

sentences.en: no, you have to adjust your vibrato or you have to press harder with the bow or what have you.
sentences.zh: 不，你得调整你的揉弦，或者你得把弓压得更紧，诸如此类。

sentences.en: So it's a constant interplay.
sentences.zh: 所以这是一个持续的相互作用。

sentences.en: The sound influences the action.
sentences.zh: 声音影响动作。

sentences.en: The action generates the sound.
sentences.zh: 动作产生声音。

sentences.en: So it's a feedback loop between the two things.
sentences.zh: 所以这两者之间是一个反馈循环。

sentences.en: And that's true for music.
sentences.zh: 音乐是如此。

sentences.en: It's true for speech.
sentences.zh: 语言也是如此。

sentences.en: It's true for other activities that might also generate sounds.
sentences.zh: 其他可能产生声音的活动也是如此。

sentences.en: Well, getting back to the question of pleasure and music, there are some people, albeit not a lot,
sentences.zh: 好的，回到快乐与音乐的话题上来，有一些人，虽然不多，

sentences.en: who don't get any pleasure from listening to music, the musical anhedonia it's called.
sentences.zh: 他们听音乐时感受不到任何快乐，这被称为音乐性快感缺失。

sentences.en: This is something that you've studied.
sentences.zh: 这是你研究过的一个课题。

sentences.en: What causes it and can it be overcome by somebody who doesn't get anything from music but would like to enjoy it?
sentences.zh: 是什么导致了这种现象？对于那些从音乐中得不到任何乐趣但又想享受音乐的人来说，能克服它吗？

sentences.en: Yeah, this is a very interesting phenomenon.
sentences.zh: 是的，这是一个非常有趣的现象。

sentences.en: We discovered it about 15 years ago or so.
sentences.zh: 我们大约在15年前发现了它。

sentences.en: Because prior to that, I mean, everyone, including us, we had the assumption, well, of course, you know, everyone loves music, right?
sentences.zh: 因为在此之前，我的意思是，每个人，包括我们，都有这样一个假设：当然啦，每个人都喜欢音乐，对吧？

sentences.en: And then we started thinking about it more seriously.
sentences.zh: 然后我们开始更严肃地思考这个问题。

sentences.en: And, you know, as scientists, you're supposed to question your own assumptions, right?
sentences.zh: 而且，你知道，作为科学家，你应该去质疑你自己的假设，对吧？

sentences.en: That's supposed to be a part of science.
sentences.zh: 这本该是科学的一部分。

sentences.en: And I have very good students, and they will often question my assumptions.
sentences.zh: 我有一些非常优秀的学生，他们经常会质疑我的假设。

sentences.en: That's part of their job.
sentences.zh: 那是他们工作的一部分。

sentences.en: And, you know, I like to encourage them to do that.
sentences.zh: 而且，你知道，我喜欢鼓励他们这么做。

sentences.en: And so, you know, one of them sort of said to me, well, how do we know that everyone likes music?
sentences.zh: 所以，你知道，其中一个人对我说，我们怎么知道人人都喜欢音乐呢？

sentences.en: And I was like, oh, well, I don't know.
sentences.zh: 我就想，哦，好吧，我不知道。

sentences.en: I'm just taking it for granted.
sentences.zh: 我只是把它当成理所当然的。

sentences.en: Well, why don't we actually find out?
sentences.zh: 我们为什么不亲自去查明真相呢？

sentences.en: So to make a long story short, we developed a series of questionnaires.
sentences.zh: 简而言之，我们开发了一系列问卷。

sentences.en: We went out into the field.
sentences.zh: 我们走到实地去。

sentences.en: We tested, you know, a few thousand people to figure it out.
sentences.zh: 我们测试了几千人来弄清这个问题。

sentences.en: And what we found, really, to my surprise, is that about something like 2% of people or so who are otherwise completely healthy, there's really nothing wrong with them.
sentences.zh: 而我们发现的（这确实让我很惊讶）大约有2%左右的人，他们在其他方面完全健康，真的没有什么不对劲。

sentences.en: I don't refer to this as a disorder exactly because they don't think there's anything wrong with them.
sentences.zh: 我并不确切地把这称为一种障碍，因为他们自己并不觉得有什么不对劲。

sentences.en: And, you know, I think it's part of neurodiversity, actually.
sentences.zh: 而且，你知道，我认为这实际上是神经多样性的一部分。

sentences.en: I don't think it should be looked on as a, you know, negative sort of thing.
sentences.zh: 我不认为这应该被视为一种，你知道的，消极的事情。

sentences.en: But these are people who report no pleasure to music, even though, importantly, they experience pleasure to everything else.
sentences.zh: 但这些人报告说他们对音乐感受不到任何快乐，尽管很重要的一点是，他们对其他所有事物都能体验到快乐。

sentences.en: And I mentioned the reward system earlier as responding to, you know, food or other pleasurable activities, including, for example, social interactions,
sentences.zh: 我刚才提到奖励系统会对，你知道的，食物或其他令人愉悦的活动做出反应，例如包括社交互动，

sentences.en: including intellectual sort of experiences, including, of course, romantic love, sex.
sentences.zh: 包括各种智力体验，当然也包括浪漫的爱、性。

sentences.en: These are things that activate the reward system.
sentences.zh: 这些都是能够激活奖励系统的事物。

sentences.en: So these people with musical antedonia, they respond to all those things.
sentences.zh: 所以这些患有音乐快感缺失症的人，他们对所有这些事物都有反应。

sentences.en: We tested them very specifically by having them play really kind of addictive video games that where you can win some money.
sentences.zh: 我们通过让他们玩那种你可以赢得一些钱的、非常容易上瘾的电子游戏来对他们进行非常具体的测试。

sentences.en: And we know this activates a reward system.
sentences.zh: 我们知道这会激活奖励系统。

sentences.en: This is why those games are annoyingly addictive, right?
sentences.zh: 这就是为什么这些游戏烦人地上瘾，对吧？

sentences.en: And when we gave those games to these people, they, you know, sort of got hooked on it just like everyone else.
sentences.zh: 当我们把这些游戏交给这些人时，他们，你知道的，就像其他人一样对它上瘾了。

sentences.en: But when we played music to them and we put them in a brain scanner, we noticed there was no response at all in their reward system or very, very limited.
sentences.zh: 但当我们在他们听音乐时把他们放入脑部扫描仪中时，我们注意到他们的奖励系统中根本没有反应，或者非常、非常有限。

sentences.en: And so this is exactly in line with what they report on questionnaires.
sentences.zh: 所以这完全符合他们在问卷中报告的内容。

sentences.en: When you ask them, they say, well, of course, I'd like to, you know, go watch a movie with my friends.
sentences.zh: 当你问他们时，他们会说，嗯，当然，我愿意，你知道的，和我的朋友们去看电影。

sentences.en: And then I'd like to go out for a meal afterwards and maybe, you know, enjoy a few beers.
sentences.zh: 然后我愿意随后出去吃顿饭，也许，你知道的，享受几杯啤酒。

sentences.en: And, you know, I have a boyfriend and I'd like to hang out with him and, you know, et cetera.
sentences.zh: 而且，你知道的，我有一个男朋友，我想和他一起出去玩，你知道的，诸如此类。

sentences.en: These are all the normal pleasures of life.
sentences.zh: 这些都是生活中正常的小确幸。

sentences.en: But when I'm with my friends and they say, oh, let's go to a concert, I'm always completely blank about it.
sentences.zh: 但当我和朋友在一起，他们说，哦，我们去听音乐会吧，我对此完全没有感觉。

sentences.en: And then they tell me, oh, you have to listen to this, you know, new band that just came out.
sentences.zh: 然后他们告诉我，哦，你必须听听这个，你知道的，刚刚出道的新乐队。

sentences.en: And they put the music on and I'm completely flat.
sentences.zh: 他们把音乐放出来，而我内心毫无波澜。

sentences.en: And I tell them, no, music just doesn't do it for me.
sentences.zh: 我告诉他们，不，音乐对我来说真的没什么感觉。

sentences.en: And so this is very interesting because it means that, you know, the way that we experience music can be dissociated from the pleasure response that we talked about earlier.
sentences.zh: 所以这非常有趣，因为这意味着，你知道的，我们体验音乐的方式可以与我们前面讨论的快乐反应分离开来。

sentences.en: And when we dig further into the brains of these folks with musical anhedonia, what we observe is that the literally the connection,
sentences.zh: 当我们进一步深入研究这些患有音乐快感缺失症的人的大脑时，我们观察到的是，字面上的连接，

sentences.en: the white matter fibers that connect the auditory part of the brain with the reward system, that system is less robust than it normally is.
sentences.zh: 连接大脑听觉部分与奖励系统的白质纤维，该系统比正常情况下要弱。

sentences.en: That pathway is not as well structured as it typically is.
sentences.zh: 该通路的结构不像典型的那样好。

sentences.en: And so we think this is very likely a congenital sort of effect.
sentences.zh: 所以我们认为这很可能是一种先天性的效应。

sentences.en: People usually tell us that this is something that they've had, you know, ever since they can remember.
sentences.zh: 人们通常告诉我们，这是他们，你知道的，从记事起就有的东西。

sentences.en: It is not a recent something that happened.
sentences.zh: 这不是最近才发生的事情。

sentences.en: And so, like I mentioned, I think it's good to think of it in terms of neurodiversity.
sentences.zh: 所以，就像我提到的，我认为从神经多样性的角度来思考它是很好的。

sentences.en: People's brains are wired in different ways.
sentences.zh: 人们的大脑是以不同的方式连接的。

sentences.en: And even though most of us are really wired for music, some of us very strongly so.
sentences.zh: 尽管我们大多数人的大脑天生就对音乐敏感，其中一些人甚至非常强烈。

sentences.en: We call them hyperhedonics.
sentences.zh: 我们称他们为超强快感者。

sentences.en: There are some people for whom music is really not emotionally engaging.
sentences.zh: 有些对人们来说音乐真的不能引起情感上的共鸣。

sentences.en: And by the way, there's nothing wrong with their auditory system either.
sentences.zh: 顺便说一句，他们的听觉系统也没有任何问题。

sentences.en: We, of course, check for that.
sentences.zh: 我们当然对此进行了检查。

sentences.en: We test for their ability to distinguish the pitch of different tones and things like that.
sentences.zh: 我们测试了他们区分不同音高以及诸如此类事情的能力。

sentences.en: So it's not that they can't hear the patterns.
sentences.zh: 所以并不是他们听不到这些模式。

sentences.en: It's just that the patterns are not especially emotionally engaging for them.
sentences.zh: 只是这些模式对他们来说没有特别的情感共鸣。

sentences.en: And given the brain's plasticity, as we now understand it, is there a way to train yourself to appreciate music if you are anhedonic?
sentences.zh: 鉴于我们现在对大脑可塑性的理解，如果你有快感缺失，有没有办法训练自己去欣赏音乐呢？

sentences.en: Yeah, that's a really good question.
sentences.zh: 是的，这是一个非常好的问题。

sentences.en: One of my colleagues is, in fact, testing that right now.
sentences.zh: 事实上，我的一个同事目前正在测试这一点。

sentences.en: I'm skeptical that it will work because if this connection that I talked about is physically not as functional as normal,
sentences.zh: 我对它是否管用持怀疑态度，因为如果我刚才谈到的这个连接在生理上不如正常情况那么功能完好，

sentences.en: then I think the absence of that pathway suggests that, to me at least, that it probably isn't something that's easy to train.
sentences.zh: 那么这条通路的缺失向我表明，至少对我来说，这可能不是一件容易通过训练改变的事情。

sentences.en: But I have to keep an open mind about it because we do know that these pathways often can be enhanced with different kinds of experience.
sentences.zh: 但我必须对此保持开放的心态，因为我们确实知道这些通路通常可以通过不同类型的体验得到增强。

sentences.en: So it is possible.
sentences.zh: 所以这是可能的。

sentences.en: I don't know.
sentences.zh: 我不知道。

sentences.en: We'll see.
sentences.zh: 我们走着瞧。

sentences.en: We'll know maybe in another year or two when my colleague's study is finished.
sentences.zh: 也许再过一两年，等我同事的研究完成时我们就知道了。

sentences.en: I mean, many of the people we talk to with musical anhedonia don't report it as any kind of hindrance to their lives.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，我们交谈过的许多患有音乐快感缺失症的人并没有将其报告为对他们生活的任何阻碍。

sentences.en: You know, they say, no, my life is perfectly fine.
sentences.zh: 你知道的，他们说，不，我的生活非常好。

sentences.en: I really, I don't get music, but it doesn't bother me.
sentences.zh: 我真的，我听不懂音乐，但这并不困扰我。

sentences.en: So, you know, I think we just have to be careful about respecting, you know, how people feel about it.
sentences.zh: 所以，你知道的，我认为我们只需要谨慎对待，尊重，你知道的，人们对此的感受。

sentences.en: It's not a disorder that needs to be cured, necessarily.
sentences.zh: 它不一定是一种需要治愈的疾病。

sentences.en: Right, right.
sentences.zh: 没错，没错。

sentences.en: Well, for a lot of people, music has an amazing ability to bring back memories.
sentences.zh: 嗯，对很多人来说，音乐具有唤起回忆的神奇能力。

sentences.en: You know, a particular song might transport us back to the moment when we first heard it or to a significant event in our life.
sentences.zh: 你知道的，一首特定的歌曲可能会把我们带回到我们第一次听到它的那一刻，或者我们生活中的一个重要事件。

sentences.en: And you were talking earlier about even just hearing a little bit of a snippet of somebody whistling a song could bring back a memory.
sentences.zh: 你刚才谈到，甚至只是听到别人吹口哨的一小段旋律就能唤起一段记忆。

sentences.en: Why is music such a powerful cue for autobiographical memory?
sentences.zh: 为什么音乐是自传体记忆如此强大的线索？

sentences.en: Yeah, this is a topic of great intereSt.
sentences.zh: 是的，这是一个非常受关注的话题。

sentences.en: And there's a lot of very good research going on right now attempting to answer that question in some detail, especially because if we can figure out why it is, why it is the case,
sentences.zh: 现在有很多非常好的研究正在试图详细回答这个问题，特别是如果我们能弄清楚原因，为什么会这样，

sentences.en: we might be able to develop certain applications, like therapeutic applications, for people with memory disorders.
sentences.zh: 我们也许能够开发出某些应用，比如针对记忆障碍人群的治疗应用。

sentences.en: So that's something that I think is important to research.
sentences.zh: 所以我认为这是值得研究的事情。

sentences.en: The short answer that I would give goes back to the reward system, because we know that the reward system is central to memory formation.
sentences.zh: 我给出的简短回答要追溯到奖励系统，因为我们知道奖励系统是记忆形成的核心。

sentences.en: I mentioned at the very beginning that reward is related to reinforcement.
sentences.zh: 我在最开始提到过，奖励与强化有关。

sentences.en: So, you know, reinforcement learning, it goes way back, you know, to in psychology, right, to the middle of the previous century.
sentences.zh: 所以，你知道的，强化学习，它可以追溯到，你知道的，在心理学中，追溯到上个世纪中叶，对吧？

sentences.en: And the idea is that you learn to perform certain actions based on how rewarding they are,
sentences.zh: 这个想法是，你根据行为带来多少奖励来学习执行某些动作，

sentences.en: which means that you're encoding information and you're encoding that information better when your dopamine levels are higher.
sentences.zh: 这意味着当你多巴胺水平较高时，你正在编码信息，并且对该信息的编码效果更好。

sentences.en: And less well when your dopamine levels are lower.
sentences.zh: 而当你的多巴胺水平较低时，编码效果较差。

sentences.en: And this makes perfect sense from a biological perspective.
sentences.zh: 从生物学的角度来看，这完全讲得通。

sentences.en: You want to remember the things that are important, the things that are salient, the things that will bring you reward compared to things that are kind of trivial or unimportant.
sentences.zh: 你想要记住那些重要的事情，那些显著的事情，那些能给你带来奖励的事情，而不是那些琐碎的或不重要的事情。

sentences.en: So it stands to reason that since music does activate the reward system, when you are listening to that music, you're in a state of heightened information processing,
sentences.zh: 因此，顺理成章的是，既然音乐确实会激活奖励系统，当你听音乐时，你就处于一种高度的信息处理状态中，

sentences.en: which leads to better memory formation.
sentences.zh: 这会带来更好的记忆形成。

sentences.en: And so that, I think, is part of the reason why we have these sometimes quite strong autobiographical sorts of effects,
sentences.zh: 所以，我认为，这就是为什么我们有时会有这种非常强烈的自传体记忆效应的部分原因，

sentences.en: because typically they're very emotionally salient events as well.
sentences.zh: 因为通常它们也是非常具有情感显著性的事件。

sentences.en: So it's the emotion generated by the music, but also the emotion generated by the event.
sentences.zh: 所以这是音乐产生的情感，也是事件本身产生的情感。

sentences.en: The two together cause an association to be formed between the music and the event, whatever it is that you're remembering.
sentences.zh: 这两者结合在一起，在音乐和事件之间建立了某种联系，无论你记住的是什么。

sentences.en: We're going to take a short break.
sentences.zh: 我们要休息一会儿。

sentences.en: When we return, I'll talk with Dr. Zatori about what makes music beautiful and whether there are any pieces of music that are considered universally beautiful.
sentences.zh: 回来后，我将与扎托里博士探讨是什么让音乐变得美丽，以及是否存在被普遍认为是美丽的音乐作品。

sentences.en: I want to talk about what makes music beautiful.
sentences.zh: 我想谈谈是什么让音乐变得美丽。

sentences.en: Now, if you Google world's most beautiful music, right, Google the source of everything, you get an amazing range of answers.
sentences.zh: 现在，如果你谷歌“世界上最美丽的音乐”，对吧，谷歌这个万事之源，你会得到令人惊叹的各种答案。

sentences.en: I mean, everything from Barbara Zadagio that I mentioned in the intro, to The Temptations, My Girl, to the soundtrack for Phantom of the Opera, for example.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，从我在引言中提到的巴伯的《柔板》，到The Temptations的《My Girl》，再到例如《歌剧魅影》的原声带。

sentences.en: But aside from the reaction of people who have anhedonia, are there any pieces of music that are universally considered beautiful?
sentences.zh: 但除了患有快感缺失症的人的反应之外，是否有任何音乐作品被普遍认为是很美的呢？

sentences.en: I would say that the answer is no, with respect to specific pieces of music.
sentences.zh: 我想说，就具体的音乐作品而言，答案是否定的。

sentences.en: I would say the answer is yes, with respect to specific principles that underlie different types of music.
sentences.zh: 我想说，就不同类型音乐背后的具体原则而言，答案是肯定的。

sentences.en: So let me unpack that for you a little bit.
sentences.zh: 所以让我为你稍微剖析一下这一点。

sentences.en: So music is extremely culturally dependent, right?
sentences.zh: 音乐具有极强的文化依赖性，对吧？

sentences.en: So when someone says that they like the Beatles, presumably this is someone who grew up in a certain time period, in a certain place, with a certain sort of cultural background.
sentences.zh: 所以当有人说他们喜欢披头士乐队时，这大概是一个在特定时期、特定地点、具有某种文化背景的人。

sentences.en: If you take someone who is, you know, a member of an isolated tribe in the Amazon forest, they have their own music, and it is probably not the Beatles.
sentences.zh: 如果你带上一个，你知道的，亚马逊森林中某个孤立部落的成员，他们有自己的音乐，那可能不是披头士。

sentences.en: And if you play the Beatles for them, they'll go, I don't know what that's about, but I prefer my flute and my drum, which are meaningful to me.
sentences.zh: 如果你给他们放披头士的歌，他们会说，我不知道这是什么，但我更喜欢我的长笛和鼓，对我有意义。

sentences.en: And this is true, right?
sentences.zh: 事实确实如此，对吧？

sentences.en: Music is present in all cultures, but differs significantly, at least in its superficial expression, in terms of the instruments that are used,
sentences.zh: 音乐存在于所有文化中，但在其表面表达上存在显着差异，就所使用的乐器而言，

sentences.en: in terms of the different scales that are used.
sentences.zh: 就所使用的不同音阶而言。

sentences.en: Because, you know, we're all familiar with the Western scale, people tend to think that's the only one that exists, but it's absolutely not the case.
sentences.zh: 因为，你知道的，我们都熟悉西方音阶，人们往往认为那是唯一存在的音阶，但事实绝对不是这样的。

sentences.en: If you listen to Indian classical music, they have ragas, which are quite different from the Western ones.
sentences.zh: 如果你听印度古典音乐，他们有拉加（raga），这与西方的音阶截然不同。

sentences.en: If you go to Indonesia, they play gamelans, which have a completely different sound structure to them, and so on and so forth for many different cultures.
sentences.zh: 如果你去印度尼西亚，他们演奏甘美冈，其声音结构完全不同，许多不同的文化也是如此。

sentences.en: The same for rhythMs.
sentences.zh: 节奏也是如此。

sentences.en: In Western music, we tend to use duple or triple meters,
sentences.zh: 在西方音乐中，我们倾向于使用二拍子或三拍子，

sentences.en: but there are certain cultures in Africa, for example, that use far more complex metrical structures, you know, meters of seven or 11,
sentences.zh: 但例如非洲的某些文化，使用的节拍结构要复杂得多，你知道的，七拍或十一拍的节拍，

sentences.en: sort of prime number metrical structure, which sounds weird to us, and we can't even reproduce it, but they can.
sentences.zh: 某种质数节拍结构，对我们来说听起来很奇怪，我们甚至无法复制它，但他们可以。

sentences.en: So what makes music beautiful?
sentences.zh: 那么是什么让音乐变得美丽呢？

sentences.en: I think there is a universal feature of what makes music beautiful, irrespective of the culture, and that is the degree to which a particular moment of music is predictable or not.
sentences.zh: 我认为音乐之所以美丽，有一个跨文化的普遍特征，那就是特定时刻的音乐在多大程度上是可预测的。

sentences.en: And there's a fundamental principle in psychology, which has been known from the time of Wilhelm Wundt in the 19th century,
sentences.zh: 心理学中有一个基本原则，自19世纪威廉·冯特的时代起就为人所知，

sentences.en: which is that you need to have a certain degree of surprise to experience something as pleasurable or important or salient, but not too much surprise and not too little surprise.
sentences.zh: 那就是你需要有一定程度的惊奇感才能将某事体验为愉悦、重要或显著，但惊奇感不能太多也不能太少。

sentences.en: So there's a curve.
sentences.zh: 所以存在一条曲线。

sentences.en: It's called the Wundt curve.
sentences.zh: 它被称为冯特曲线。

sentences.en: He published it in 1887, I think, and it's been demonstrated many, many times since.
sentences.zh: 我想他在1887年发表了它，从那以后它已经被演示过很多很多次了。

sentences.en: So what does it mean?
sentences.zh: 那这意味着什么呢？

sentences.en: It means that the brain is constantly trying to interpret what it receives from the environment and trying to anticipate what the next thing will be that's coming.
sentences.zh: 这意味着大脑一直在试图解释它从环境中接收到的东西，并试图预测接下来会发生什么。

sentences.en: This, again, goes back to a very fundamental survival mechanism.
sentences.zh: 这同样可以追溯到非常基本的生存机制。

sentences.en: If you're in an environment and you see a sequence of events, you want to be able to know what's going to happen next so that you can be prepared to take the right action.
sentences.zh: 如果你身处某种环境中并看到一系列事件，你希望能够知道接下来会发生什么，以便你能准备好采取正确的行动。

sentences.en: The right action might be to pounce and grab the prey and eat it, or the right action might be to run away as fast as you can,
sentences.zh: 正确的行动可能是扑过去抓住猎物并吃掉它，或者正确的行动可能是尽可能快地逃跑，

sentences.en: or the right action might be to approach another member of your species with some proposal for lovemaking or something like that.
sentences.zh: 或者正确的行动可能是带着某种要求爱抚之类的提议接近你物种的另一个成员。

sentences.en: These are all very different actions, but you're always trying to anticipate what's happening.
sentences.zh: 这些都是非常不同的行动，但你总是在试图预测正在发生的事情。

sentences.en: Now, music is kind of a microcosm of that because music consists of a sequence of elements over time that are unfolding over time,
sentences.zh: 现在，音乐可以说是这一切的缩影，因为音乐由随时间推移而展开的一系列元素组成，

sentences.en: and they follow a certain pattern depending on your culture.
sentences.zh: 并且它们根据你的文化遵循某种模式。

sentences.en: It might be a rhythmic pattern of a certain type.
sentences.zh: 它可能是某种类型的节奏模式。

sentences.en: It might be a scale structure of a certain type.
sentences.zh: 它可能是某种类型的音阶结构。

sentences.en: Those differ across cultures,
sentences.zh: 这些在不同的文化中有所不同，

sentences.en: but across all of them, you always have some degree of expectation about what will happen, and the musician knows this implicitly.
sentences.zh: 但在所有这些文化中，你对接下来会发生什么总会有一定程度的期望，音乐家对此心知肚明。

sentences.en: Every musician I've ever talked to, whenever I explain this whole theory, they go, well, yeah, of course, we know this.
sentences.zh: 我交谈过的每一位音乐家，每当我解释这个完整的理论时，他们都会说，哦，是的，当然，我们知道这一点。

sentences.en: You know, this is what we do.
sentences.zh: 你知道的，这就是我们的工作。

sentences.en: We give you something a little different than what you were expecting.
sentences.zh: 我们给你一些与你预期的略有不同的东西。

sentences.en: We don't just give you the identical thing because that's boring.
sentences.zh: 我们不会只给你完全相同的东西，因为那太无聊了。

sentences.en: If I play something like a major scale,
sentences.zh: 如果我演奏某种大调音阶，

sentences.en: if I play a major scale, you know, da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da, super boring.
sentences.zh: 如果我演奏一个大调音阶，你知道的，哆来咪发索啦西哆，超级无聊。

sentences.en: Like, no one would listen to that.
sentences.zh: 就像，没人会听那个。

sentences.en: Why?
sentences.zh: 为什么？

sentences.en: Because it's too predictable.
sentences.zh: 因为它太可预测了。

sentences.en: You know exactly what's going to happen at every moment.
sentences.zh: 你确切地知道每个时刻会发生什么。

sentences.en: If I play you a bunch of completely random notes, complete chaos, that's also totally boring.
sentences.zh: 如果我给你演奏一堆完全随机的音符，完全混乱，那也完全无聊。

sentences.en: Why?
sentences.zh: 为什么？

sentences.en: Because it's also unpredictable.
sentences.zh: 因为它也是不可预测的。

sentences.en: There's no structure, so you cannot predict what's going to happen.
sentences.zh: 没有任何结构，所以你无法预测会发生什么。

sentences.en: But there's a sweet spot that Wilhelm Bundt identified, which is the balance between predictability and surprise.
sentences.zh: 但威廉·冯特确定了一个最佳平衡点，即在可预测性和惊奇感之间的平衡。

sentences.en: So you want some surprise, but you also need some predictability.
sentences.zh: 所以你需要一些惊喜，但你也需要一些可预测性。

sentences.en: In fact, in order to get surprise, you need to have predictability.
sentences.zh: 事实上，为了获得惊喜，你需要具备可预测性。

sentences.en: In order to be surprised, you have to be expecting that something's going to happen.
sentences.zh: 为了感到惊讶，你必须预期会发生某些事情。

sentences.en: If you're completely lost without knowing what's going on, you can't be surprised because you have no expectation about what's going to happen.
sentences.zh: 如果你完全迷失了方向，不知道发生了什么，你就无法感到惊讶，因为你对接下来会发生什么没有任何期望。

sentences.en: So I think this is the key to what makes music and other art forms as well.
sentences.zh: 所以我认为这是让音乐以及其他艺术形式变得美妙的关键。

sentences.en: People have applied this theory to poetry, for example, or to humor.
sentences.zh: 人们已经将这个理论应用到了诗歌或幽默中。

sentences.en: You know, we have some, like the punchline is an unexpected event.
sentences.zh: 你知道的，我们有一些，比如妙语就是一件意想不到的事情。

sentences.en: Even to visual art, people have tried this.
sentences.zh: 人们甚至尝试将之应用于视觉艺术。

sentences.en: And I think that the reward system, coming back to that idea, is we know this from experiments.
sentences.zh: 我认为奖励系统，回到这个概念，我们从实验中知道了这一点。

sentences.en: We know that it's extremely sensitive to obtaining rewards that are unexpected.
sentences.zh: 我们知道它对获得意料之外的奖励极其敏感。

sentences.en: So I mentioned, you know, the classical experiments where you're measuring dopamine from, let's say, a rodent as it receives food.
sentences.zh: 所以我提到过，你知道的，经典实验中，比如你在啮齿动物接受食物时测量多巴胺。

sentences.en: And sure, there's a response.
sentences.zh: 当然，会有反应。

sentences.en: But what's even more interesting is that you can condition that response on an unrelated stimulus.
sentences.zh: 但更有趣的是，你可以将这种反应条件反射到一个无关的刺激上。

sentences.en: Like, let's say, a light goes on that signals that food will come.
sentences.zh: 比如，假设亮起一盏灯，预示着食物将要到来。

sentences.en: And the reward system will, once the animal is trained, will respond to that signal earlier in time.
sentences.zh: 一旦动物接受了训练，奖励系统就会在时间上更早地对该信号做出反应。

sentences.en: And then if the reward that it receives
sentences.zh: 然后，如果它收到的奖励

sentences.en: is larger than usual, you'll get a huge boost in the dopamine response.
sentences.zh: 比平时更大，你的多巴胺反应就会得到巨大的提升。

sentences.en: So this is what our reward system is sensitive to.
sentences.zh: 这就是我们的奖励系统所敏感的东西。

sentences.en: It's sensitive to the reward you're experiencing in relation to the cues that preceded it, the cues that predicted it.
sentences.zh: 它对你所经历的奖励很敏感，这个奖励与之前的提示以及预测它的提示有关。

sentences.en: So if you're following the music and you make a certain prediction and then the musician plays a different chord that, let's say, modulates into a different key
sentences.zh: 所以如果你跟着音乐走，并做出某种预测，然后音乐家弹奏了一个不同的和弦，比方说，转调到了一个不同的调式

sentences.en: or there's the entrance of a new voice, for instance, right?
sentences.zh: 或者出现了一个新的声音，比如说，对吧？

sentences.en: You're hearing, you know, the bass guitar and then the singer comes in at a certain moment, maybe a slightly unexpected moment.
sentences.zh: 你听到的是，你知道的，贝斯吉他，然后歌手在某个时刻切入，也许是一个稍微意想不到的时刻。

sentences.en: These are the kinds of moments of music that people find super pleasurable and it can be related back to these very fundamental mechanisms where you are surprised.
sentences.zh: 这些正是人们觉得超级愉悦的音乐时刻，这可以追溯到那些让你感到惊讶的非常基础的机制。

sentences.en: You were expecting something, but what you got was even better than what you were expecting.
sentences.zh: 你原本期待着某些东西，但你得到的甚至比你期待的还要好。

sentences.en: And that's where dopamine really kicks in and gives you pleasure.
sentences.zh: 这就是多巴胺真正发挥作用并带给你快感的地方。

sentences.en: I'm wondering if there is a connection between musical ability and language aptitude, since music is, in effect, a type of language.
sentences.zh: 我想知道音乐能力和语言倾向之间是否存在某种联系，因为音乐实际上是一种语言。

sentences.en: And it's also a type of mathematics.
sentences.zh: 而且它也是一种数学。

sentences.en: I mean, you can't really play music without having some fundamental, intrinsic understanding of math.
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，如果不具备对数学的某些基础的、内在的理解，你其实是无法演奏音乐的。

sentences.en: Do you see these connections neurologically?
sentences.zh: 你在神经学上看到了这些联系吗？

sentences.en: Yes and no.
sentences.zh: 算有，也算没有。

sentences.en: I think we do see some relationships between these different functions, but not in the way that people usually think about it.
sentences.zh: 我认为我们确实看到了这些不同功能之间的一些关系，但并不是人们通常所想的那种方式。

sentences.en: So a common idea that's out there that people are promoting because they can make money from it is that, oh, well, if you give your kid music lessons,
sentences.zh: 所以人们经常宣传的一种观点是，因为他们可以从中赚钱，那就是，哦，好吧，如果你让你的孩子去上音乐课，

sentences.en: they'll do better in math class.
sentences.zh: 他们在数学课上就会表现得更好。

sentences.en: I'm not terribly convinced
sentences.zh: 我并不是非常坚信

sentences.en: by the evidence for that.
sentences.zh: 这方面的证据。

sentences.en: And besides, if your goal is to make the kid be better at math, they should take math lessons, not music lessons.
sentences.zh: 况且，如果你的目标是让孩子的数学更好，他们应该去上数学课，而不是音乐课。

sentences.en: I think music lessons are fantastic because music is fantastic, not because it's good for math.
sentences.zh: 我认为音乐课非常棒，因为音乐本身就很棒，而不是因为它对数学有帮助。

sentences.en: So to me, that's not quite the right thing.
sentences.zh: 所以在看来，这并不完全是那么回事。

sentences.en: Having said that, we do know that there are certain cognitive operations in the brain that are relevant for both music making and for something like math.
sentences.zh: 话虽如此，我们确实知道大脑中某些认知操作与音乐创作和诸如数学之类的事情都是相关的。

sentences.en: And I'll give you an example.
sentences.zh: 我给你举个例子。

sentences.en: So there's a part of the brain, the parietal lobe, which we know is important for doing sort of what mathematicians would call coordinate transforMs.
sentences.zh: 所以大脑中有一个部分，顶叶，我们知道它对于做某种数学家所谓的坐标变换非常重要。

sentences.en: So that could be as simple as recognizing an object when it's in one orientation and then you rotate it to another orientation and you recognize that it's the same object.
sentences.zh: 所以这可能很简单，比如当一个物体处于某个方向时识别它，然后你把它旋转到另一个方向，并认出它还是同一个物体。

sentences.en: So this part of the brain in the parietal lobe is responsible for things like that that we do very automatically and take for granted.
sentences.zh: 因此，顶叶中的这部分大脑负责我们做得非常自然且视为理所当然的事情。

sentences.en: You can extend that to actual math.
sentences.zh: 你可以把它延伸到实际的数学中。

sentences.en: So doing geometry, for instance, or geometric theorems or, I don't know, matrix algebra, there are many aspects of math that would involve similar kinds of computations.
sentences.zh: 比如做几何，或者几何定理，或者，我不知道，矩阵代数，数学中有许多方面会涉及类似性质的计算。

sentences.en: It turns out that there are also musical computations.
sentences.zh: 事实证明，也有音乐计算。

sentences.en: These are implicit computations, right?
sentences.zh: 这些是内隐计算，对吧？

sentences.en: Like you're not aware of it.
sentences.zh: 就像你并没有意识到一样。

sentences.en: Like when you recognize the object in different orientations, you're not thinking to yourself, oh, there's a rotation of 37.6 degrees, you know, which corresponds
sentences.zh: 就像当你以不同方向识别物体时，你并不是在对自己说，哦，这里旋转了37.6度，你知道的，这对应着

sentences.en: to this, you know, transform.
sentences.zh: 这个，你知道的，变换。

sentences.en: No, you just recognize it.
sentences.zh: 不，你只是认出来了。

sentences.en: Your brain is doing the math.
sentences.zh: 你的大脑在做数学运算。

sentences.en: You're not actually, you don't have access,
sentences.zh: 你其实并没有，你没有接触到，

sentences.en: conscious access to those operations.
sentences.zh: 对这些操作的有意识接触。

sentences.en: And some years ago we started thinking, well, what's the musical equivalent of moving an object in space?
sentences.zh: 几年前我们开始思考，嗯，在空间中移动物体的音乐对应物是什么？

sentences.en: And we thought, oh,
sentences.zh: 我们想，哦，

sentences.en: what's an object?
sentences.zh: 什么是物体？

sentences.en: Well, let's say a melody.
sentences.zh: 嗯，比方说一段旋律。

sentences.en: How do you move it?
sentences.zh: 你如何移动它？

sentences.en: Well, it doesn't move in space, but it can move in pitch.
sentences.zh: 嗯，它不在空间中移动，但它可以在音高上移动。

sentences.en: And musicians call that transposition,
sentences.zh: 音乐家称之为移调，

sentences.en: right?
sentences.zh: 对吧？

sentences.en: This is a very commonplace function that you can recognize the same tune if it's sung in different registers, for instance, right?
sentences.zh: 这是一个非常普通的功能，比如如果用不同的音区演唱，你也能认出同一首曲子，对吧？

sentences.en: That doesn't take any special musical training ability.
sentences.zh: 这不需要任何特殊的音乐训练能力。

sentences.en: A child can do that without any special training.
sentences.zh: 一个小孩子不需要任何特殊的训练就能做到这一点。

sentences.en: But if you think about what's going on, think about the pitches of each of the tones, right?
sentences.zh: 但如果你想想正在发生的事情，想想每个音调的音高，对吧？

sentences.en: If I take,
sentences.zh: 如果我拿，

sentences.en: let's say, a major chord,
sentences.zh: 比方说，一个大三和弦，

sentences.en: C, E, G, right?
sentences.zh: C，E，G，对吧？

sentences.en: If I now transpose it to,
sentences.zh: 如果我现在把它移调到，

sentences.en: I don't know, let's say, the key of F sharp, now it's going to be
sentences.zh: 我不知道，比方说，升F大调，现在它将变成

sentences.en: F sharp,
sentences.zh: 升F，

sentences.en: A sharp,
sentences.zh: 升A，

sentences.en: C sharp.
sentences.zh: 升C。

sentences.en: All the tones are completely different, but you still recognize that the intervals are the same, exactly.
sentences.zh: 所有的音完全不同，但你依然能准确地认出音程是相同的。

sentences.en: The relationships between each pair of tones is the same.
sentences.zh: 每一对音之间的关系是相同的。

sentences.en: Technically, it's the frequency ratios between them.
sentences.zh: 严格来说，是它们之间的频率比。

sentences.en: So, when we do experiments where we ask people to recognize this is a major chord or not in different keys, what we see is that the same region of the parietal lobe
sentences.zh: 所以，当我们做实验，要求人们在不同的调式中识别这是否是一个大三和弦时，我们看到的是顶叶的同一区域

sentences.en: is actually active as has been identified for things like visual rotation.
sentences.zh: 实际上是活跃的，就像在诸如视觉旋转等事情中被识别出的那样。

sentences.en: And so that's an example of a link between mathematical operations that apply in music and that apply in other domains.
sentences.zh: 所以这就是应用于音乐以及应用于其他领域的数学运算之间联系的一个例子。

sentences.en: And so that, I think, is kind of a deep similarity between the two.
sentences.zh: 因此，我认为，这是两者之间的一种深层相似性。

sentences.en: Another area of music that has interested me for a long time is musical autodidacts, the people who become highly proficient at music, but they never really had
sentences.zh: 音乐的另一个领域长期以来一直让我感兴趣，那就是音乐自学者，那些在音乐上变得非常精通，但从未真正接受过

sentences.en: any formal training.
sentences.zh: 任何正规训练的人。

sentences.en: And there are a lot of people on that liSt.
sentences.zh: 那个名单上有很多人。

sentences.en: I mean, in popular music, we've got
sentences.zh: 我的意思是，在流行音乐中，我们有

sentences.en: Jimi Hendrix,
sentences.zh: 吉米·亨德里克斯，

sentences.en: Eric Clapton, and classical musicians like Edward Elgar,
sentences.zh: 埃里克·克莱普顿，还有古典音乐家如爱德华·埃尔加，

sentences.en: Telemann.
sentences.zh: 泰勒曼。

sentences.en: What is happening in the brains of autodidacts that's different from the rest of us who have to take lessons and practice and practice and practice and never really get great?
sentences.zh: 自学成才者的脑子里到底发生了什么，这与我们这些必须上课、练习、练习、再练习却从未真正变得伟大的人有什么不同？

sentences.en: Yeah, it's a great question.
sentences.zh: 是的，这是一个很好的问题。

sentences.en: I don't think we know the answer fully, but I think it's a very interesting question because it gets at the issue of individual differences in musical ability.
sentences.zh: 我认为我们并不完全知道答案，但我认为这是一个非常有趣的问题，因为它触及了音乐能力个体差异的问题。

sentences.en: we do see that if you take a random group of
sentences.zh: 我们确实发现，如果你随机抽取一组

sentences.en: 100 people, you're going to have all kinds of variability in their musical capacities.
sentences.zh: 100人，他们的音乐能力将存在各种各样的差异。

sentences.en: So 2% of them might have musical antedonia, another 3% or 4% might have what we call amusia, which is sort of tone deafness, but then another
sentences.zh: 所以其中2%的人可能患有音乐失歌症，另外3%或4%的人可能患有所谓的失歌症，也就是某种程度上的音盲，但接着另外

sentences.en: 5% will just be very, very good at something simple like sending back a tune.
sentences.zh: 5%的人在像回放曲调这样简单的事情上会非常非常擅长。

sentences.en: So we all know that
sentences.zh: 所以我们都知道

sentences.en: little kids can sing back tunes actually
sentences.zh: 小孩子其实从小就能

sentences.en: surprisingly well from an early age, but we all know that there are some kids who will not just sing it back, but sing it back with beautiful
sentences.zh: 出奇好地回放曲调，但我们也知道有些孩子不仅仅是回放，而且回放时具有塑造音高并且非常、非常精准等美妙的

sentences.en: ability to shape the tones and to be very, very on pitch and so on.
sentences.zh: 能力。

sentences.en: So there's this wide range of abilities out there.
sentences.zh: 所以存在着如此广泛的能力范围。

sentences.en: Most of us are somewhere in the middle
